lines.trans: Sasha, is everything ready for the festive banquet?
Yes, the guests are already sitting at the table.
Has the chef already finished cooking the main dish?
The cooks are just now carrying the roasted goose.
Excellent, it is time to congratulate the birthday girl!
Shall we light beautiful candles on the cake?
Yes, and open the most expensive champagne.
The judge looks very happy today.
She is a strict person, but loves attention.
Her husband gave her a magnificent bouquet of flowers.
I hope our restaurant gives her joy.
All the waiters are ready to greet guests with a smile.
Then we begin the celebration at the highest level!

meanings.note: a large formal meal for many people

examples.text: У нас сегодня очень важный банкет.
examples.trans: We have a very important banquet today.
A lavish banquet was hosted in the restaurant.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'dish', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: This is the restaurant's signature dish.

examples.text: Настоящий повар чувствует каждый вкус блюда.
examples.trans: A real chef feels every taste of the dish.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bouquet' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He brought a bouquet of flowers.

examples.text: Я пришёл просить прощения. Я принёс этот букет.
examples.trans: I came to ask for forgiveness. I brought this bouquet.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('magnificent, splendid').

examples.trans: A magnificent idea from an unknown person.

examples.text: Муж подарил ей великолепный букет цветов.
examples.trans: Her husband gave her a magnificent bouquet of flowers.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Прошу внимания = May I have your attention

meanings.en: to meet, to greet, to pick up
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'тречать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to meet, to welcome', paired with 'встретить'.

examples.text: Вас и не должны были встречать.
examples.trans: Nobody was supposed to meet you.

examples.text: Он всегда встречает гостей у двери.
examples.trans: He always greets guests at the door.

examples.text: Это не накладка. Вас и не должны были встречать.
examples.trans: That's not a mix-up. Nobody was supposed to meet you.

meanings.note: ends a conversation or an order: 'Всё, свободен' = that's all, you can go
Secondary conversational sense ('that's it, done') (at the start of a sentence) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'глядеть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look'.

examples.trans: On top the costume looks simply super!

examples.text: Не говорите так, вы прекрасно выглядите!
examples.trans: Do not say that, you look wonderful!

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'high', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'main' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('the main thing') (neuter главное, used as a noun) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The main thing is, don't worry.
The most important thing is the people.

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to prepare') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: usually the short form: я готов (m), я готова (f)
a large waterbird with a long neck and webbed feet

examples.trans: Chef, this is a live goose!

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
to a loved one, and at the start of letters
to a loved one, and at the start of letters

examples.text: В Москве вам дают деньги на дорогую одежду, а мозги не дают.
examples.trans: In Moscow they give you money for expensive clothes, but they don't give you brains.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'жечь'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to light, ignite', paired with 'зажигать'.

examples.text: Мы зажжём красивые свечи на торте?
examples.trans: Shall we light beautiful candles on the cake?

examples.text: Пусть официанты зажгут красивые свечи на столах.
examples.trans: Let the waiters light beautiful candles on the tables.

meanings.en: to finish, to end, to complete
meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'кончить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to finish', forming an aspectual pair with 'заканчивать'.

examples.trans: I want to finish what I started.

examples.text: Был неправ. Простите. Я хочу закончить начатое.
examples.trans: I was wrong. Forgive me. I want to finish what I started.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'печённый'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('roasted, baked').

examples.text: Повара как раз несут запечённого гуся.
examples.trans: The cooks are just now carrying the roasted goose.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common feminine noun meaning 'birthday girl' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Excellent, it is time to congratulate the birthday girl!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'to' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('beautiful, handsome').

examples.trans: They have a very beautiful house.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to love, to like', paired with 'полюбить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to like') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'husband', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Nina, pour your husband a drink. We've got something to celebrate!

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'деяться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hope, to rely on', paired with 'понадеяться'.

examples.trans: I hope so. Go on, act quickly!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'чинать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to begin, to start', paired with 'начать'.

examples.text: Аркаш, ну что скажешь? Когда начинать?
examples.trans: Arkasha, so what do you say? When do I start?

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: one direction, now; 'Неси!' = Bring (it)!

examples.trans: Yulia, bring a pen and a piece of paper.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'крыть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to open', forming an aspectual pair with 'открывать'.

examples.trans: Open the door. Is this flat nine?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'excellently'.
Secondary conversational sense ('great!, excellent!') (as a one-word reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I know this town really well!

meanings.note: From German 'Offiziant' / Late Latin 'officians' (one who performs a duty or service).

examples.trans: The waiter politely greets the new guests.
Please do not block the walkway for the waiters.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'арить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to give (as a present)', paired with 'дарить'.

examples.text: А вы мне тоже айфон подарите?
examples.trans: Will you give me an iPhone too?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'здравлять'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to congratulate', forming an aspectual pair with 'поздравить'.
+ infinitive: Пора идти = Time to go

examples.trans: It's time for us to go.
All right, Arkashenka. We'll be off, it's time.

meanings.note: Новый год — мой любимый праздник = New Year is my favourite holiday
Secondary conversational sense ('celebration, party') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: New Year is a family holiday.

examples.text: Это семейный праздник. Как в детстве, с подарками!
examples.trans: It's a family holiday. Like when we were kids, with presents!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('festive, holiday').

examples.trans: Chef, the festive dessert is already ready!

examples.text: Саша, всё готово к праздничному банкету?
examples.trans: Sasha, is everything ready for the festive banquet?

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'joy'.

examples.text: Он бы сейчас до потолка прыгал от радости.
examples.trans: He would be jumping to the ceiling for joy right now.
What a joy to see you!

examples.text: Мы с радостью сообщаем вам новость. Ваш долг полностью аннулирован!
examples.trans: We gladly inform you of the news. Your debt is completely canceled!

meanings.note: 'один раз' = once, 'два раза' = twice
Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: forms the superlative: самый главный = the most important
Secondary conversational sense ('the very') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The most important thing is the people.
Do you know the main thing?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'веча'). Common feminine noun meaning 'candle' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я приношу бутылку шампанского и свечи.
examples.trans: I'll bring a bottle of champagne and candles.
Candles are burning on the table.

examples.text: Прекрасно! Я приношу бутылку шампанского и свечи.
examples.trans: Wonderful! I'll bring a bottle of champagne and candles.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'идеть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to sit', forming an aspectual pair with 'посидеть'.

examples.trans: Why are you sitting in the corner?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'table', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: We will sit together in a friendly way at the table.

examples.text: Не бойся, всё в порядке! Посидим дружно за столом.
examples.trans: Don't be afraid, everything is fine! We will sit together in a friendly way at the table.
Take your feet off the table quickly!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трогий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strict, stern').

examples.trans: How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

examples.text: У нас в школе очень строгий директор.
examples.trans: We have a very strict principal at our school.

examples.text: Ой, спина не разгибается! Какая вы строгая, Клавдия Викторовна.
examples.trans: Ow, my back won't straighten! How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

meanings.note: in a court of law or a referee in sport

examples.trans: Wait. And who is the judge?

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'happy', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('lucky') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('happy (ending)') (счастливый конец = happy ending) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The film has a happy ending.

examples.text: Ты сейчас один против всех. Счастливого конца не будет.
examples.trans: Right now you're alone against everyone. There won't be a happy ending.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cake', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: А ты готовишь мой любимый торт со сгущёнкой!
examples.trans: And you make my favourite condensed milk cake!

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'лыбка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'smile' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Все официанты готовы встречать гостей улыбкой.
examples.trans: All the waiters are ready to greet guests with a smile.

examples.text: У тебя мои глаза и улыбка.
examples.trans: You have my eyes and smile.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'ровень'). Common masculine noun meaning 'level' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Экскаваторщик — это не мой уровень. Может, поможешь?
examples.trans: Excavator driver isn't my level. Maybe you could help?

meanings.note: plural цветы is used for cut flowers / a bouquet
the plural is a different word: люди, людям, о людях
Secondary conversational sense ('people') (plural люди, a different word) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: declined like an adjective; no plural in normal use

examples.text: Там же президент выступает! Надо открыть шампанское.
examples.trans: But the president is on TV! We have to open the champagne.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.
